newsitem.title: USA: Indiana governor calls for overhaul of state taxes.
newsitem.headline: Indiana governor calls for overhaul of state taxes.

text.p: Indiana Gov. Frank O'Bannon called for an overhaul of state taxes in his state of the state speech Tuesday evening before the legislature.

O'Bannon, a Democrat and former lieutenent governor who won the Nov. 5 gubernatorial race, said he will appoint a citizens commission on taxes to examine the state's "entire tax structure, top to bottom."
Included in that review will be the state's method of assessing property taxes, he said.

The Indiana Supreme Court last month overturned a state tax court ruling found the system to be unconstitutional because it was not based solely on fair market valuation. The high court returned the case to the tax court to detemine whether the current system results in non-uniform and unequal property valuations.
O'Bannon outlined his own tax relief plan that would "tighten the cap" on local property tax increases to save taxpayers more than $200 million over the next four years.

Mark D. Brown, deputy state budget director, said the plan would decrease the annual allowed levy growth for local governments, except schools, to a minimum of four percent from five percent to a maximum of eight percent from 10 percent.

The rest of O'Bannon's tax cut plan would also provide income tax credits equal to property tax payments to residents depending on their annual income. In addition, the governor's plan would increase the renter's tax deduction by $1,000, provide a welfare-to-work income tax credit.

Brown said the governor's entire tax cut package is expected to cost more than $700 million over four years. He added that funding for the cuts would be covered by the state's surplus revenues, which totaled $1.7 billion at the end of fiscal 1996.

Brown said that under a proposed fiscal $16.8 billion 1998-99 general fund biennial budget submitted to the legislature earlier this month, the tax cuts would decrease the projected combined balances at the end of fiscal 1999 to just under $1 billion.
